lesson.title: The Mirror Test: Recognizing Symmetric Distributions
lesson.summary: A symmetric distribution has matching halves on either side of its center, which makes the mean and median nearly equal and gives you a baseline for judging every other shape in this unit.
lesson.body:
A distribution is symmetric when its left half is a mirror image of its right half around a central point. Picture folding a histogram or dotplot down the middle: if the two sides land almost exactly on top of each other, the distribution is symmetric. This is one of the four things you always describe when discussing the shape of a distribution, alongside center, spread, and unusual features like outliers, and it is usually the very first judgment call you make when you look at a graph.

Symmetry matters because it tells you something powerful about how the mean and median relate to each other. In a symmetric distribution, values are balanced on both sides of the center: for every data point sitting a certain distance above the center, there tends to be a matching point roughly the same distance below it. Those matched pairs pull the arithmetic average in opposite directions by equal amounts, so the pulls cancel out and the mean lands at essentially the same spot as the median. This is why "mean equals median, roughly" is the standard test statisticians use to check whether a distribution behaves symmetrically, without needing to draw a picture at all.

Consider five quiz scores: 60, 70, 80, 90, and 100. Arranged in order, the middle value, the median, is 80. Now compute the mean: 60 + 70 + 80 + 90 + 100 = 400, and 400 divided by 5 is 80. The mean and median match exactly. Look at the distances from the center: negative 20, negative 10, 0, positive 10, positive 20. Each low score has a matching high score the same distance away, which is exactly the mirror-image pattern that defines symmetry.

A more elaborate example comes from rolling two fair six-sided dice and recording the sum. The possible totals run from 2 to 12, and the frequency of each total mirrors around 7: a sum of 2 and a sum of 12 each happen in only one way, rolling a 1 and a 1 or a 6 and a 6, a sum of 3 and a sum of 11 each happen in two ways, and so on, up through a sum of 7, the most common outcome, which can happen in six different ways out of the 36 equally likely combinations. Because every low total has a matching high total occurring with the same frequency, this distribution balances perfectly around 7, giving it the mirror pattern of symmetry even though it has a single peak in the middle rather than a flat top like some symmetric shapes.

Perfect symmetry like this is rare in real data. Heights of adult women, standardized test scores across a large population, and measurement errors in a science lab all tend to pile up near a typical value and taper off in both directions at similar rates, producing shapes that are approximately symmetric rather than exactly symmetric. Statisticians are comfortable calling a distribution symmetric even when the match is close but imperfect, as long as there is no long stretched out tail favoring one side.

Symmetry is also the reference point for everything that follows in this unit. When a distribution is not symmetric, it is skewed, and the direction of the skew is named after the side with the longer tail. A symmetric distribution can still take different forms underneath, it might have one central peak or two separate peaks, but the defining feature discussed here is only the left right balance. Once you can recognize balance, you are ready to recognize its absence, which is exactly what skewed left and skewed right distributions represent.
